lesson.title: Relations and functions: equivalence relations, one-one and onto functions

blocks.text: Relations: domain, codomain, range and counting

A **relation** links elements of one set to elements of another. Everyday examples are "is a brother of" on a set of people or "is less than" on numbers. In mathematics we record a relation as a set of ordered pairs.

A **relation** $R$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $A\times B$. If $(a,b)\in R$ we write $aRb$ and say $a$ is related to $b$. A relation **on** a set $A$ means a relation from $A$ to $A$, that is, a subset of $A\times A$.

The set $A$ is the **domain** of the relation (the set of first components allowed), $B$ is the **codomain**, and the **range** is the set of second components that actually occur in $R$. The range is always a subset of the codomain.

blocks.latex: n(A\times B)=n(A)\,n(B),\qquad \text{number of relations from }A\text{ to }B=2^{\,n(A)\,n(B)}
blocks.text: $A\times B$ has $n(A)\,n(B)$ ordered pairs, and each pair can be either in or out of a relation, so the number of subsets is $2^{n(A)n(B)}$ (this count includes the empty relation and the universal relation $A\times B$). For a relation on a set with $n$ elements the count is $2^{n^2}$.

blocks.problem: Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{a,b\}$. How many relations from $A$ to $B$ exist? List the relation $R=\{(x,y): x \text{ is odd}\}$.
blocks.solution: $n(A)=3$ and $n(B)=2$, so $n(A\times B)=6$ and the number of relations is $2^6=64$. The odd elements of $A$ are $1$ and $3$, and $y$ can be $a$ or $b$, so $R=\{(1,a),(1,b),(3,a),(3,b)\}$. Its domain (as a set of used first components) is $\{1,3\}$ and its range is $\{a,b\}$.

blocks.text: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive relations
A relation $R$ on $A$ is **reflexive** if $(a,a)\in R$ for **every** $a\in A$. One missing pair $(a,a)$ destroys reflexivity.
$R$ is **symmetric** if $(a,b)\in R\Rightarrow(b,a)\in R$ for all $a,b\in A$. Pairs of the form $(a,a)$ satisfy this automatically.

$R$ is **transitive** if $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,c)\in R\Rightarrow(a,c)\in R$ for all $a,b,c\in A$. The condition only demands a pair when a chain $a\to b\to c$ exists; with no such chain it holds vacuously.

rows: A pair $(a,b)$, $a\ne b$, has no mirror
A chain exists without the shortcut pair

blocks.problem: On $A=\{1,2,3\}$ let $R=\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2)\}$. Decide whether $R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
blocks.solution: **Reflexive:** $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)$ are all present, so yes. **Symmetric:** $(1,2)\in R$ but $(2,1)\notin R$, so no. **Transitive:** the chains are $(1,1),(1,2)\Rightarrow(1,2)\in R$; $(1,2),(2,2)\Rightarrow(1,2)\in R$; all chains using only diagonal pairs are trivial. So it is transitive.

blocks.text: To prove a property is false you need only one counter-example. To prove it true for a rule like "a - b is divisible by 5" you must give a general argument that works for all elements.

**Counting facts** for a set with $n$ elements: a relation is reflexive when all $n$ diagonal pairs are present, leaving $n^2-n$ pairs free, so there are $2^{n^2-n}$ reflexive relations. A symmetric relation chooses each unordered pair $\{a,b\}$ and each diagonal pair freely: $n+\binom n2=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2$ choices, so there are $2^{n(n+1)/2}$ symmetric relations. Reflexive **and** symmetric relations have the diagonal forced and only the $\binom n2$ unordered pairs free: $2^{n(n-1)/2}$.
Equivalence relations and equivalence classes
A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive** is called an **equivalence relation**. It groups related elements together as "equal for some purpose".

Standard examples of equivalence relations: equality on any set; "has the same remainder on division by $n$" (congruence modulo $n$) on the integers; "is parallel to" on lines; "has the same birthday as". Standard non-examples: "$\le$" on $\mathbb R$ (not symmetric), "divides" on $\mathbb N$ (not symmetric), "is perpendicular to" on lines (not reflexive, not transitive).
For an equivalence relation $R$ on $A$, the **equivalence class** of $a$ is $[a]=\{x\in A: xRa\}$. Two classes are either identical or disjoint, and the distinct classes together **partition** $A$.

blocks.problem: On $\mathbb Z$ define $aRb$ if $a-b$ is divisible by $5$. Show that $R$ is an equivalence relation and find the number of distinct equivalence classes. Write the class of $2$.
blocks.solution: **Reflexive:** $a-a=0$ is divisible by $5$. **Symmetric:** if $5\mid(a-b)$ then $5\mid(b-a)=-(a-b)$. **Transitive:** if $5\mid(a-b)$ and $5\mid(b-c)$ then $5\mid[(a-b)+(b-c)]=(a-c)$. So $R$ is an equivalence relation. Related integers leave the same remainder when divided by $5$, and the possible remainders are $0,1,2,3,4$, so there are $5$ classes. $[2]=\{\dots,-8,-3,2,7,12,\dots\}$.

blocks.text: Because classes partition a set, the number of equivalence relations on a set equals the number of ways to partition it. For $\{1,2,3\}$ the partitions are $\{1\}\{2\}\{3\}$; $\{1,2\}\{3\}$; $\{1,3\}\{2\}$; $\{2,3\}\{1\}$; $\{1,2,3\}$ — so there are exactly $5$ equivalence relations.

A relation can be symmetric and transitive yet fail reflexivity if some element is related to nothing. For example R = {(1,2),(2,1),(1,1),(2,2)} on {1,2,3} is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive because (3,3) is missing.
Functions: one to one and onto

A **function** $f:A\to B$ is a relation in which **each** element of $A$ is related to **exactly one** element of $B$. We write $f(a)=b$; $b$ is the **image** of $a$ and $a$ a **pre-image** of $b$. $A$ is the domain, $B$ the codomain and $\{f(x):x\in A\}$ the range.
$f$ is **one to one** if different elements of the domain have different images: $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Equivalently, no two arrows land on the same element.
$f$ is **onto** if every element of the codomain has at least one pre-image: range $=$ codomain. For every $y\in B$ the equation $f(x)=y$ must have a solution $x\in A$.

A function that is both one to one and onto is **bijective** (a one-one correspondence). Whether a function is one-one or onto depends on the domain and codomain chosen, not only on the formula. For instance $f(x)=x^2$ is not one-one on $\mathbb R$ (since $f(2)=f(-2)$) and not onto $\mathbb R$ (negative numbers are never obtained), but it is one-one on $[0,\infty)$ and onto $[0,\infty)$.

blocks.problem: Show that $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=3x-7$ is one-one and onto.
blocks.solution: **One-one:** if $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ then $3x_1-7=3x_2-7$, so $3x_1=3x_2$ and $x_1=x_2$. **Onto:** take any $y\in\mathbb R$ and solve $3x-7=y$, giving $x=\dfrac{y+7}{3}\in\mathbb R$, and $f\!\left(\dfrac{y+7}{3}\right)=y$. Every real number has a pre-image, so $f$ is onto. Hence $f$ is bijective.

blocks.latex: \#\text{ functions }A\to B=m^{\,n},\quad \#\text{ one-one}=\frac{m!}{(m-n)!}\ (m\ge n),\quad \#\text{ onto }(n=3\text{ or }4,\ m=2)=2^{n}-2
blocks.text: Here $n=n(A)$ and $m=n(B)$. A function chooses an image in $B$ for each of the $n$ elements of $A$: $m^n$ ways. A one-one function chooses distinct images: $m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)$ ways, and is impossible if $n>m$. A function into a 2-element set is onto unless all elements go to the same image, so the number of onto functions onto a 2-element codomain is $2^n-2$.

For a function from a **finite set to itself**, one-one and onto are equivalent: if the $n$ elements of $A$ go to $n$ distinct elements of $A$, all of $A$ is used. This is false for infinite sets: $x\mapsto2x$ on $\mathbb N$ is one-one but not onto.

blocks.problem: How many one-one functions are there from $\{1,2,3\}$ to $\{a,b,c,d\}$? How many onto functions from $\{1,2,3,4\}$ to $\{p,q\}$?
blocks.solution: One-one: $1$ has $4$ choices of image, $2$ has $3$ remaining, $3$ has $2$ remaining, so $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$. Onto: there are $2^4=16$ functions in all; the two constant functions (all to $p$, all to $q$) are not onto, leaving $16-2=14$.

blocks.text: A relation on A is a subset of A x A. Reflexive: all (a,a) present. Symmetric: pairs come with mirrors. Transitive: chains close up. Equivalence = all three, and it splits the set into disjoint classes.
One-one: different inputs, different outputs (f(x1) = f(x2) implies x1 = x2). Onto: range = codomain. A bijection is both. Always check the stated domain and codomain.
With n(A) = 3: relations 2^9; reflexive 2^6 = 64; symmetric 2^6 = 64; reflexive and symmetric 2^3 = 8; equivalence relations 5.
To show a function is NOT one-one, give two different inputs with the same output. To show it is NOT onto, give one element of the codomain that is never obtained.

questions.stem: Set A has 2 elements and set B has 3 elements. How many relations from A to B exist?
questions.explanation: A relation from A to B is any subset of A x B. Here n(A x B) = 2 x 3 = 6, and a set with 6 elements has 2^6 = 64 subsets. So there are 64 relations including the empty relation and the whole of A x B.

optionRationale.2: 6 is the size of A x B, not the number of subsets of it.
optionRationale.3: This is 2^5; the exponent must be n(A)n(B) = 6.
optionRationale.4: 9 is the number of functions from A to B (3^2), not relations.

questions.objective: Count the relations between two finite sets

questions.stem: On the set {1, 2, 3} the relation R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)} is
options: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.explanation: All of (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) belong to R, so R is reflexive. The pair (1,2) is in R but (2,1) is not, so R is not symmetric. Every chain (a,b),(b,c) in R gives (a,c) in R, as the only non-diagonal chain (1,2),(2,2) yields (1,2). So R is transitive.

optionRationale.2: All diagonal pairs are present, so R is reflexive.
optionRationale.3: The chain (1,2),(2,2) gives (1,2), which is present, so R is transitive.
optionRationale.4: (1,2) is present but (2,1) is not, so R is not symmetric and hence not an equivalence relation.

questions.objective: Classify a relation given as a set of ordered pairs

questions.stem: Which of the following functions from R to R is one-one?
questions.explanation: If 2x1 + 3 = 2x2 + 3 then x1 = x2, so 2x + 3 is one-one. The other three functions each take the same value at x and -x: x^2, |x| and x^2 + 1 all satisfy f(1) = f(-1), so none of them is one-one on R.

optionRationale.1: f(2) = f(-2) = 4, so it is not one-one.
optionRationale.2: f(1) = f(-1) = 1, so it is not one-one.
optionRationale.3: f(1) = f(-1) = 2, so it is not one-one.

questions.objective: Identify a one-one function

questions.stem: Match the property of a relation R on a set A in List-I with its meaning in List-II.

right: I. (a,b) in R and (b,c) in R implies (a,c) in R
II. (a,a) in R for every a in A
IV. (a,b) in R implies (b,a) in R

questions.explanation: Reflexive means every element is related to itself (II). Symmetric means a related pair can be reversed (IV). Transitive means chains close up, (a,b) and (b,c) force (a,c) (I). An equivalence relation has all three properties (III). So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.
questions.objective: Match relation properties with their definitions

questions.stem: The function f: N -> N defined by f(x) = 2x is
questions.explanation: If 2x1 = 2x2 then x1 = x2, so f is one-one. But every output 2x is even, so an odd number such as 3 in the codomain N has no pre-image: 2x = 3 has no natural solution. Hence f is not onto.

optionRationale.1: 2x1 = 2x2 forces x1 = x2, so it is one-one.
optionRationale.3: Odd numbers have no pre-image, so it is not onto.
optionRationale.4: It is one-one, so it cannot be neither.

questions.objective: Test a function on the natural numbers for one-one and onto

questions.stem: The number of reflexive relations on a set with 3 elements is
questions.explanation: A relation on a 3-element set is a subset of the 9 pairs of A x A. For reflexivity the 3 diagonal pairs (a,a) must be included, leaving 9 - 3 = 6 pairs that may be chosen freely. So there are 2^6 = 64 reflexive relations.

optionRationale.2: 512 = 2^9 is the number of all relations on the set.
optionRationale.4: 128 = 2^7 does not correspond to 9 - 3 = 6 free pairs.

questions.objective: Count reflexive relations

questions.stem: On Z, define aRb if a - b is divisible by 5. The number of distinct equivalence classes of R is
questions.explanation: Two integers are related exactly when they leave the same remainder when divided by 5. The possible remainders are 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, and each gives one class, for example [2] = {..., -3, 2, 7, 12, ...}. These five classes are disjoint and together cover Z.

optionRationale.1: The remainders 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 give five classes, not four.
optionRationale.2: There is no class for remainders 5 to 9 since they repeat.
optionRationale.3: Each class itself is infinite, but there are only five classes.

questions.objective: Find the number of equivalence classes of congruence modulo n

questions.stem:
For the relation R on the set N of natural numbers defined by aRb if a divides b, consider:
A. R is reflexive.
B. R is symmetric.
C. R is transitive.
D. R is an equivalence relation.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Every natural number divides itself, so R is reflexive (A true). If a divides b and b divides c then a divides c, so R is transitive (C true). But 2 divides 4 while 4 does not divide 2, so R is not symmetric (B false), and hence it is not an equivalence relation (D false).

optionRationale.1: 2 divides 4 but 4 does not divide 2, so R is not symmetric.
optionRationale.2: R is reflexive and R is not symmetric, so this is wrong in both ways.
optionRationale.4: R is not symmetric, so A, B and C cannot all hold.

questions.objective: Test a divisibility relation for the three properties

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** The relation R = {(1,2), (2,1)} on the set {1, 2} is symmetric but not transitive.
**Reason (R):** (1,2) and (2,1) belong to R but (1,1) does not belong to R.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Each pair has its mirror, so R is symmetric. For transitivity, the chain (1,2), (2,1) requires (1,1) to be in R, but (1,1) is absent. So R is not transitive. The reason states exactly this missing pair, so it explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is not merely true; (1,1) missing is exactly why transitivity fails.
optionRationale.3: R is true: (1,1) is indeed absent from R.
optionRationale.4: A is true; the symmetry holds and the failure of transitivity is genuine.

questions.objective: Show a relation is symmetric but not transitive

questions.stem: The number of one-one functions from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b, c, d} is
questions.explanation: Choose images one element at a time with no repetition. Element 1 can go to any of 4 elements, element 2 to any of the remaining 3, and element 3 to any of the remaining 2. The number of one-one functions is 4 x 3 x 2 = 24, which equals 4!/(4-3)!.

optionRationale.1: 64 = 4^3 counts all functions, including repeated images.
optionRationale.4: 81 = 3^4 swaps the roles of the sets.

questions.objective: Count one-one functions between finite sets

questions.stem: The number of onto functions from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} is
questions.explanation: There are 2^3 = 8 functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set. Exactly two of them are constant (everything to a, or everything to b) and miss one element of the codomain, so they are not onto. Hence there are 8 - 2 = 6 onto functions.

optionRationale.2: 8 = 2^3 counts all functions including the two constant ones.
optionRationale.3: 2 counts only the constant functions, which are not onto.

questions.objective: Count onto functions onto a two-element set

questions.stem: For f: R -> R given by f(x) = x^2 + 1, the function becomes onto if the codomain R is replaced by
questions.explanation: Since x^2 is at least 0 for real x, x^2 + 1 is at least 1, with value 1 attained at x = 0, and every larger value is attained (x = sqrt(y - 1)). So the range is [1, infinity) and the function is onto exactly when the codomain equals its range.

optionRationale.1: The smallest value of x^2 + 1 is 1, so values in [0,1) are never obtained.
optionRationale.2: The value 1 is attained at x = 0 so it must be included.

questions.objective: Identify the range of a function

questions.stem: On the set N x N, define (a,b) R (c,d) if ad = bc. Which pair is related to (2, 3)?
questions.explanation: For (a,b) = (2,3) and (c,d) = (4,6) the condition ad = bc reads 2 x 6 = 12 and 3 x 4 = 12, which are equal, so (4,6) is related. For (6,4): 8 against 18; for (3,2): 4 against 9; for (5,7): 14 against 15, so none of these is related.
questions.objective: Apply an equivalence relation defined on pairs

questions.stem: Consider f: R -> R defined by f(x) = x^3 - x. Then f is
questions.explanation: f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1 - 1 = 0, so two different inputs share the output 0 and f is not one-one. The cubic tends to -infinity as x goes to -infinity and to +infinity as x goes to +infinity and is continuous, so every real value is attained: f is onto.

optionRationale.1: f(0) = f(1) = 0, so it is not one-one.
optionRationale.3: A cubic polynomial is continuous and takes all real values, so f is onto.
optionRationale.4: f is onto, so it cannot be neither.

questions.objective: Test a cubic function for one-one and onto

questions.stem: The number of equivalence relations on the set {1, 2, 3} is
questions.explanation: An equivalence relation corresponds to a partition of the set into classes. The partitions of {1,2,3} are {1}{2}{3}; {1,2}{3}; {1,3}{2}; {2,3}{1}; and {1,2,3}. That gives 5 partitions and hence 5 equivalence relations.

optionRationale.2: This misses the identity relation or the universal relation.
optionRationale.3: This misses one of the partitions of the set.
optionRationale.4: 8 counts reflexive and symmetric relations, not equivalence relations.

questions.objective: Count equivalence relations via partitions

questions.stem: Let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. The minimum number of ordered pairs that must be added to R to make it an equivalence relation is
questions.explanation: R is transitive but not reflexive and not symmetric. Reflexivity needs (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), and symmetry needs (2,1), (3,2), (3,1), that is 6 new pairs. After adding them R contains all 9 pairs of A x A, which is an equivalence relation, so at least 6 pairs are required.

optionRationale.1: Three pairs fix reflexivity only; symmetry is still missing.
optionRationale.2: This misses one pair of the full relation.
optionRationale.3: This misses one pair of the full relation.

questions.objective: Extend a relation to an equivalence relation

questions.stem:
**Assertion (A):** Every one-one function from a finite set A to itself is onto.
**Reason (R):** A one-one function maps the n distinct elements of A to n distinct elements of A, which exhausts A.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: If |A| = n, a one-one function sends the n elements to n pairwise distinct elements of A. Since A has only n elements, these images are all of A, so the function is onto. The reason gives the proof, so both statements are true with R explaining A. The result fails for infinite sets.

optionRationale.2: R is the actual argument for A, not a separate fact.
optionRationale.3: R is true: n distinct images in an n-element set fill it.
optionRationale.4: A is true for finite sets.

questions.objective: Link one-one and onto for finite sets

questions.stem: The number of onto functions from {1, 2, 3, 4} to {p, q} is
questions.explanation: There are 2^4 = 16 functions from a 4-element set to a 2-element set. The only functions that are not onto are the two constant functions (all elements to p or all to q). So the number of onto functions is 16 - 2 = 14.

optionRationale.1: 16 = 2^4 counts all functions, including both constant ones.

questions.objective: Count onto functions using total minus constant

questions.stem:
On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, let R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3)}. Consider:
A. R is an equivalence relation.
B. The equivalence class of 3 is {3, 4}.
C. R has exactly three equivalence classes.
D. (1,3) belongs to R because of transitivity.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: R contains all diagonal pairs, each non-diagonal pair has its mirror, and the only chains are inside {1,2} and inside {3,4}, so R is an equivalence relation (A true). The class of 3 is {3,4} (B true). There are two classes, {1,2} and {3,4}, so C is false, and no chain links 1 to 3, so D is false.

optionRationale.1: C is false: the classes are {1,2} and {3,4}, only two.
optionRationale.3: D is false: no chain connects 1 to 3, so (1,3) is not forced; also A is true and missing.
optionRationale.4: C is false, and B is also true.

questions.objective: Analyse an equivalence relation and its classes

questions.stem: The number of relations on a set with 3 elements that are both reflexive and symmetric is
questions.explanation: The diagonal pairs are forced by reflexivity. The 6 off-diagonal ordered pairs fall into 3 mirror pairs {(a,b),(b,a)}, and symmetry says each mirror pair is either entirely present or entirely absent. So there are 2^3 = 8 such relations.

optionRationale.2: 64 counts reflexive relations only, without the symmetry requirement.
optionRationale.3: 6 is the number of off-diagonal ordered pairs, not the count of relations.
optionRationale.4: 512 is the count of all relations on the set.

questions.objective: Count relations that are reflexive and symmetric
